newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin doctors say may fix heart surgery any day.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin doctors say may fix heart surgery any day.

text.p: Preparations for President Boris Yeltsin's heart bypass operation moved ahead on Friday and his spokesman said doctors could decide on surgery "any day".
Yeltsin has been waiting since early September while doctors have treated him for anaemia, a thyroid problem and other ailments.
All meetings with the 65-year-old president have been cancelled but he remains formally in charge of affairs of state.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference that Yeltsin's doctors were meeting daily and could fix the operation date at any of their sessions.

U.S. specialist Michael DeBakey, expected in Moscow this weekend, has predicted a target date of next week, but Yastrzhembsky declined to confirm this. Doctors initially indicated mid-November as the most likely time.
Yeltsin is still in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, awaiting transfer to the Cardiological Institute in the city's western suburbs where the multiple bypass operation will take place.
DeBakey, an 88-year-old pioneer of open heart surgery, will advise Russian doctors but will not be present in the operating theatre itself, the Kremlin spokesman said.
Yastrzhembsky told reporters Yeltsin had signed an order giving Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin temporary authority to sign power-sharing agreements with Russia's regions.
But Chernomyrdin is likely to assume full presidential powers, including control of Russia's nuclear arsenal, only just before Yeltsin goes under the knife.

Yastrzhembsky told reporters he personally sympathised with the view of top surgeon Renat Akchurin, who will lead the operation team, that it was not necessary to make public in advance the date and time of the operation, which will last several hours.

"The press will be told about the start of the operation," he said, suggesting the information would not necessarily be announced in advance. But he promised that Yeltsin's handover of powers to Chernomyrdin would be made public immediately.

Top Russian officials have appeared keen to project an atmosphere of "business as usual" in the runup to the operation. Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Friday there were no plans for extra police patrols in the capital.
He told Interfax news agency his ministry was working normally and "we are sure everything will turn out all right".

Chernomyrdin spent Friday in the provincial city of Ryazan visiting airborne troops with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who told journalists the premier was "deeply concerned by the state of affairs in the army".

Unpaid wages and other payments have led to warnings that of a virtual collapse in the armed forces. The airborne troops are a special focus of discontent because of plans to cut their numbers and reorganise them.
Itar-Tass news agency reported that soldiers visited by Chernomyrdin were paid their July wages on the eve of his trip.
